text: This is Carbon Gap. Let me show you how it works, in under three minutes.

Carbon has a price, but emissions are self-declared. The moment you open Carbon Gap, you see the headline: independent data sees six billion tonnes more than countries declare. That is about what the United States emits in a year.
Every country is coloured by its gap: what it declared to the UN, versus what satellites and asset models observe, for the same year. Hatched countries have no recent declaration in our data.

Click a country. China declared fourteen point three billion tonnes for 2021. One of our research agents found that figure in its first transparency report. Independent estimates see sixteen point four. Further down, its climate commitments, researched with GPT web search.
Each country shows its largest emitting sites. This is Bełchatów, Europe's biggest coal plant, seen from space.
Now, ask the analyst anything. It runs on GPT five point five with function calling. It reads our data, searches the web and a curated knowledge base, and moves the map while it answers.
One click writes a sourced dossier, with structured outputs, and a spoken briefing.
Companies work the same way: their tracked sites, versus the Scope one emissions they report. Coal India reports twenty-seven million tonnes. Its own tracked mines emit sixty-six.
Not in the list? Type any company. An agent profiles it with web search, finds its sites in Climate TRACE, and pulls the figure it reports, with the exact quote.
Missing data? Launch a swarm of research agents. They read official reports in parallel, and every figure must come with a verbatim quote from its source.
In the EU carbon market, we show who has to buy allowances. Poland's plants must buy seventy-six million a year, while its steel and cement sectors get more free allowances than they emit.
And you can simply talk to it.
Every finding becomes a card you can share.
Carbon Gap. Carbon has a price. It deserved a check.
